person.name: Hans_Erlwein
person.summary: Hans Erlwein (1872–1914) was a German architect and municipal building official who served as Stadtbaurat of Dresden from 1905 until his death. Working between late historicism and reform-oriented vernacular approaches, he directed a wide program of public construction and coordinated collaborations with contemporary artists for integrated architectural design.

chapters.headline: Blueprints Before Fame
chapters.bridge_statement: A provincial beginning quietly sharpens into a hunger for form, order, and civic purpose.

chapters.headline: Service in Stone
chapters.bridge_statement: Training gives way to real responsibility, where public rules and real materials test ambition.

chapters.headline: Bamberg Command Post
chapters.bridge_statement: Sudden authority arrives early, and the city’s daily needs become his first true canvas.

chapters.headline: Capital of Consequence
chapters.bridge_statement: A larger city opens its gates, demanding not just buildings, but a vision of modern administration.

chapters.headline: Dresden Made Visible
chapters.bridge_statement: With the machinery of the city behind him, his ideas begin to harden into landmarks.

conclusion: Hans Erlwein turned municipal necessity into civic dignity, proving that utility can carry beauty without apology. His career ended abruptly, but Dresden still bears the outline of his disciplined imagination.

events.title: Birth in Bayerisch Gmain
events.description: Hans Erlwein (full name: Johann Jakob Erlwein) was born on 13 June 1872 in Bayerisch Gmain. He was the son of the hotelier Johann Jakob Erlwein and his wife, Elise.

events.title: Studied architecture in Munich
events.description: In 1893, Erlwein began studying architecture at the [[Technical University of Munich|Technical University in Munich]], where he received formal training in design and construction. During his student years he also joined the [[Corps Germania München|Corps Germania München]], expanding his network beyond his academic circle.

Technical University of Munich.explanation: Munich’s main technical university (today the Technical University of Munich, TUM), a leading German institution for engineering and architecture education.

Corps Germania München.explanation: A Munich student corps (traditional German student fraternity) in the Weinheim Seniors’ Convent, known for lifelong member networks among students and alumni.

events.title: Entered Bavarian building service
events.description: After completing his studies, Erlwein undertook study trips and entered public building administration in Bavaria. He worked for the [[Royal Bavarian State Railways|Royal Bavarian State Railways]], at the Landbauamt in Amberg, and as a [[Regierungsbauführer|Regierungsbauführer]] in the Bavarian military building administration, gaining practical experience in state construction.

Royal Bavarian State Railways.explanation: The state-owned railway administration of the Kingdom of Bavaria, responsible for planning, building, and operating rail infrastructure before the creation of the Deutsche Reichsbahn.

Regierungsbauführer.explanation: A German civil-service training rank for architects/engineers preparing for higher state building service (a stage on the path to becoming a Regierungsbaumeister).

events.title: Appointed Bamberg Stadtbaurat
events.description: In 1898, despite his youth and limited senior experience, Hans Erlwein was appointed [[Stadtbaurat|Stadtbaurat]] of Bamberg, placing him in charge of municipal building planning and oversight and giving him responsibility for the city’s public construction agenda.

Stadtbaurat.explanation: A German municipal office roughly equivalent to a city building director, responsible for urban construction administration and planning.

events.title: Married Marie Hirsch
events.description: In 1899, Erlwein married Marie Hirsch. Together they had a daughter, as his municipal career accelerated.

location_coordinates.label: Bamberg (inference)
location_coordinates.name: Bamberg, Bavaria, Germany
location_coordinates.source: Logical inference from Wikipedia timeline: he was Stadtbaurat in Bamberg in 1898–1904; wedding location not explicitly stated in provided cache.

events.title: Built Bamberg municipal works
events.description: In Bamberg, Hans Erlwein designed and carried out municipal commissions including a major school building and public-utility infrastructure such as an electricity works and new cattle and slaughter facilities, working within the city’s administrative and budget constraints.

images.caption: Klohäuschen by Hans Erlwein in Bamberg promenade

Bamberg.explanation: A historic Franconian city in Bavaria whose preserved medieval and baroque core made new civic building projects architecturally sensitive.

events.title: Relocated to Dresden
events.description: On 17 November 1904, Erlwein left his municipal post in Bamberg to take up the position of [[Stadtbaurat|Stadtbaurat]] in Dresden, entering a larger city administration in the capital of the [[Kingdom of Saxony|Kingdom of Saxony]].

Stadtbaurat.explanation: A senior municipal office in German cities responsible for public building and urban planning, typically heading the city’s building department.

Kingdom of Saxony.explanation: A constituent monarchy of the German Empire (1871–1918), with Dresden as its capital during Erlwein’s appointment.

events.title: Led Dresden Hochbauamt
events.description: In February 1905, Erlwein took over as head of Dresden’s [[Hochbauamt|Hochbauamt]], entering the city magistrate and overseeing municipal building projects. He also gained influence through civic roles dealing with building policy and art—such as chairing the city’s building and art committees—and through involvement in efforts supporting Dresden’s higher education.

Hochbauamt.explanation: A municipal ‘high building’ office responsible for major public building works (as distinct from roads or civil-engineering departments).

events.title: Received Red Eagle Order
events.description: In autumn 1905, Erlwein received the Prussian [[Order of the Red Eagle|Order of the Red Eagle]] (4th Class), a state decoration recognizing his service and professional standing shortly after his move to Saxony.

images.caption: Order of the Red Eagle (Prussian order insignia)

Order of the Red Eagle.explanation: A Prussian order of chivalry awarded to military and civilian officials for meritorious service and achievement; its 4th Class was a common grade for distinguished civil servants.

events.title: Designed Dresden slaughterhouse
events.description: In 1906, Erlwein began planning and constructing Dresden’s [[Städtischer Vieh- und Schlachthof|municipal livestock and slaughterhouse complex]], conceiving it as a city-run facility with disciplined circulation, hygienic workflows, and representative public architecture. In Dresden he repeatedly drew younger artists into these municipal projects—among them sculptor Georg Wrba and painters Otto Gussmann and Paul Rößler—so that functional buildings could read as unified civic works rather than mere infrastructure.

Städtischer Vieh- und Schlachthof.explanation: Dresden’s municipal livestock market and slaughterhouse complex (often called the Erlwein-Schlachthof), a major early-20th-century public-works project.

events.title: Named honorary professor
events.description: In 1910, the [[Technical University of Dresden|Technical University of Dresden]] appointed Erlwein an honorary professor, formalizing his ties to academic architectural training while he continued to lead Dresden’s municipal building office.

Technical University of Dresden.explanation: Major technical university in Dresden (today Technische Universität Dresden), one of Germany’s long-established engineering and architecture institutions.

events.title: Built Italian Village inn
events.description: In 1911, Erlwein designed and supervised the construction of the restaurant known as the [[Italienisches Dörfchen|“Italienisches Dörfchen”]] in Dresden’s central cultural area, coordinating the building work and working with artists on interior and decorative elements in line with contemporary ideas of integrated design.

Italienisches Dörfchen.explanation: A historic restaurant building in Dresden, designed by Hans Erlwein and opened in 1911 near the city’s main cultural landmarks.

events.title: Published municipal building booklet
events.description: In 1913, while serving as Dresden’s city building director, Erlwein issued a booklet outlining his approach to municipal utility architecture based on recent work for the city. In the same year he also published a separate piece on the Italienisches Dörfchen project in a contemporary architectural forum.

Italienisches Dörfchen.explanation: A small riverside building complex in Dresden (literally “Italian Village”), created in the early 1910s as part of the area’s urban redevelopment and later known as a prominent local landmark near the Semperoper.

event_class.title: Einfache städtische Nutzbauten in Dresden
event_class.impact: The text articulated design priorities for functional municipal construction and circulated them beyond Dresden’s administration.

events.title: Died in car accident
events.description: Erlwein died on 9 October 1914 in Amagne-Lucquy, near Rethel in the Ardennes, aged 42. He was killed in an automobile accident while taking part in a privately organized transport of clothing, food, and gifts intended for German soldiers on the [[Western Front|Western Front]]. His grave is in the soldiers’ cemetery at Noyers-Pont-Maugis.

Western Front.explanation: The principal theatre of World War I in western Europe, running mainly through northern France and Belgium, where German and Allied armies faced each other from 1914 onward.
